steps: Hold your dominant hand up near the side of your head.
Wave it gently from side to side with your palm facing outward.
Keep eye contact and smile while you wave.
tip: The same wave is also used for 'hi' and 'bye' in BSL.

steps: Raise your dominant hand near the side of your head, palm facing outward.
Wave it gently from side to side.
Hold eye contact briefly, then turn away naturally.
tip: 'Bye' uses the same wave; keep the movement relaxed, not exaggerated.

steps: Touch the fingertips of your flat dominant hand to your chin.
Move your hand down and away from your face in one smooth motion.
Mouth the words 'thank you' silently as you sign.
tip: A small, quick movement is all you need in everyday conversation.

steps: Touch the fingertips of your flat dominant hand to your chin.
Move your hand slightly forward and away from your face.
Mouth the word 'please' silently as you sign, since this is what distinguishes it from 'thank you'.
tip: 'Please' and 'thank you' share the same manual sign in BSL; the mouth pattern carries the meaning.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a fist.
Hold the fist against the centre of your chest.
Move it in small circles against your chest.
tip: Mouth 'sorry' silently while signing to make it unmistakable.

steps: Close your hand into a fist.
Nod the fist up and down, like a head nodding.
Repeat the nodding motion a couple of times.
tip: Pair the fist nod with an affirmative facial expression.

steps: Extend your index and middle fingers.
Tap them against your thumb, like a mouth opening and closing as it says 'no'.
Add a slight head shake for emphasis if you like.
tip: The tapping fingers look like lips mouthing the word 'no' — that visual link makes it easy to remember.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat with the palm facing up.
Rest your dominant closed hand, thumb up, on top of that flat palm.
Keep the position steady, or lift it slightly.
tip: The thumbs-up resting on the open palm reads visually as 'lifting someone up'.

steps: Raise your dominant hand, palm facing outward, fingers together.
Push it firmly forward toward the person or thing you want to stop.
Keep your expression serious to match a 'halt' command.
tip: BSL has no single all-purpose 'stop': this is the halt command. For 'stop an activity', BSL signs more like CEASE/FINISH.

steps: Bend the index finger of your dominant hand into a hook.
Start with the hand in front of your body.
Pull the bent finger toward yourself, like beckoning.
tip: Repeat the pull for emphasis, e.g. calling someone from a distance.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat, palm facing your chest.
Slide it down your chest, then twist your wrist so the palm turns outward.
tip: Add a slight forward lean and a wanting expression on your face to sell the meaning.

steps: BSL uses the same sign for NEED as for WANT.
Hold your dominant hand flat, palm facing your chest.
Slide it down your chest, finishing with a small outward twist of the wrist.
tip: Since NEED shares its sign with WANT, sign extra context around it so your meaning is clear.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat with fingers together, thumb folded across (a closed flat hand).
Tap your chest with it once or twice.
tip: Mouth the English word 'like' silently as you tap — mouthing is normal and expected in BSL.

steps: Make a fist with your thumb sticking out.
Tap the side of your head with your thumb, repeating the tap.
tip: Make the thumb tap land visibly on the head — a vague wave near the face will not read clearly.

steps: Make the KNOW sign: fist with thumb out, tapping the side of your head.
While signing, shake your head side to side with a slight frown.
In BSL the headshake itself carries the negation — it happens during the sign, not after it.
tip: Practise the headshake as part of the sign from day one; BSL negation is simultaneous, not sequential.

steps: Form the BSL letter M with your dominant hand.
Tap it against your open non-dominant palm twice.
tip: Practise the two-handed BSL M shape on its own first, so the double tap lands cleanly on the palm.

steps: Hold out your non-dominant hand with just the index and middle fingers extended.
Tap those two fingers twice with the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand — this is the BSL letter F signed twice.
tip: Keep the two taps on the same fingertips and crisp; sloppy contact can look like a different sign.

steps: Hold both hands in front of your body, one resting over the other, arms bent as if cradling something.
Rock your hands gently from side to side, like holding a baby.
tip: Slow the rocking right down when learning — the cradling mime reads best at half speed.

steps: Clasp your non-dominant hand with your dominant hand in front of your body.
Make a small up-and-down bobbing movement with the clasped hands.
tip: Keep the bob small and gentle — a big shake looks like washing your hands.

steps: Extend only the index finger of your dominant hand.
Brush it along your chin, moving from your dominant side toward the other side.
tip: Use the chin, not the cheek — BOY and GIRL live on different parts of the face.

steps: Make a closed fist with your index finger pointing up.
Brush the finger down your cheek twice.
tip: Practise BOY then GIRL back to back — cheek versus chin — to lock in the difference.

steps: Bring your fingertips and thumb together into a bunched shape.
Tap the bunched fingers against your mouth twice.
tip: Make the double tap rhythmic, like taking two bites — the timing makes it instantly readable.

steps: Curve your dominant hand into a loose C shape, as if holding a cup.
Lift the hand up to your mouth.
Tip your wrist toward your face, as though taking a drink from the cup.
tip: Keep the motion small and repeat it once or twice; mouthing the word 'drink' helps hearing learners remember it.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat, fingers together and palm facing down.
Place the hand at the front of your throat.
Make two short downward movements against the throat.
tip: The contact is light — a gentle tap against the throat, not a squeeze.

steps: Place your dominant hand flat on your stomach.
Rub the stomach in a small circular motion a few times.
Add a hungry facial expression to reinforce the meaning.
tip: A small circle is enough — big sweeping movements look exaggerated rather than natural.

steps: Bring your dominant hand, held flat, up to your throat.
Sweep the hand downward across the throat.
Repeat the downward movement once more for emphasis.
tip: Keep the fingers together and the sweep short; the throat location is what carries the meaning.

steps: Hold both hands in a closed flat shape, fingertips touching thumbs.
Place your dominant hand just in front of the other at chest height.
Tap the dominant hand against the non-dominant hand repeatedly.
tip: Two or three taps in a steady rhythm reads most naturally; mouthing 'more' helps beginners.

steps: Open both hands, palms facing each other.
Tap the palm of your dominant hand against the palm of your non-dominant hand.
Repeat the tap twice with a bright, happy facial expression.
tip: The facial expression does half the work — smile while you sign it, or it reads flat.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat and vertical in front of your face, thumb tucked in.
Drag the hand downward from nose level to chin level.
Wear a sad expression while you sign.
tip: Let your face droop slightly — in BSL the expression carries the emotion, not just the hands.

steps: Curl both hands into claw shapes, fingertips bent.
Place the claws on your chest.
Drag both hands upward and outward, away from your body, with an angry face.
tip: Keep the movement firm and decisive — a weak, slow movement reads as frustration rather than anger.

steps: Place both hands in closed flat shapes on your chest, thumbs touching the chest.
Twist both hands downward until the palms rest flat against your chest.
Let your shoulders and head droop slightly with a weary expression.
tip: Exaggerate the droop of the shoulders — the sinking body language is what makes 'tired' readable.

steps: Extend the little finger of each hand, keeping the other fingers closed.
Rest the edges of both little fingers on your chest.
Brush both little fingers downward along your body, then repeat the movement once.
tip: Think of the little fingers as sickness draining downward out of the body — that image fixes the movement in memory.

steps: Hold both hands open in front of your body, palms facing toward you.
Move the hands alternately up and down.
Add a grimace that matches the severity of the pain.
tip: Bigger alternating movements and a stronger grimace read as worse pain — scale the expression to the meaning.

steps: Curl both hands into claw shapes.
Tap both claws against your chest repeatedly.
Widen your eyes with a frightened expression.
tip: Tap quickly for a startled 'scared'; tap more slowly for a lingering sense of fear.

steps: Flatten both hands, palms facing inward.
Cross both hands over your chest on the left side.
Give a small warm press inward with a gentle smile.
tip: Think of pressing something precious to your heart — that is the image the sign is built on.

steps: Bend the fingers of your dominant hand so the fingertips point downward.
Tap your fingertips against the far side of your chest.
Then tap them against the near side of your chest.
tip: Tap lightly with the fingertips, not the whole hand, and keep your elbow relaxed.

steps: Hold both hands open in front of your body with palms facing inward.
Move both hands downward together until they finish flat and horizontal.
tip: The same sign also covers 'dark' — lower the hands smoothly, as if night is falling.

steps: Hold both hands out in front of you, palms facing up, fingers together and flat.
Bounce both hands up and down together in unison, repeating the motion.
tip: Keep both hands moving together at the same speed — the repetition marks 'right now'.

steps: Hold your non-dominant arm in front of you with the wrist facing up.
Tap the top of that wrist twice with your dominant index finger.
tip: Tap where a watch would sit — the sign points at the wrist as if checking the time.

steps: Hold your dominant index finger up in front of your body.
Wiggle your hand in short side-to-side movements.
Keep a questioning expression on your face while you sign.
tip: The facial expression is part of the sign — raise your eyebrows to mark it as a question.

steps: Hold your non-dominant arm out in front of you.
With your dominant thumb, draw a small cross on top of your opposite forearm.
tip: Only one written BSL source was found for this sign, and hospital signs vary regionally — confirm the local variant with a Deaf signer.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out flat, palm facing up.
Tap the inside edge of that palm twice with your dominant index finger.
tip: BSL uses the TOILET sign for 'bathroom' — the dictionary has no separate bathroom sign.

steps: Hold both hands up in front of you with fingers closed, as if gripping a steering wheel.
Move both hands up and down in opposite directions, like turning the wheel.
tip: Keep the movements small and alternating — it mimes turning a steering wheel.

steps: Hold both flat hands up at an angle in front of you, fingertips pointing up.
Bring the fingertips together so your hands form the shape of a roof.
tip: The same sign also covers 'home'.

steps: Hold your dominant hand up with index and middle fingers extended together.
Bend your wrist side to side while moving your hand downward.
tip: Keep the two fingers pressed together as your hand travels down.

steps: Point to yourself over your heart to sign 'I'.
Flatten both hands and cross them gently over your chest, as if pressing something into your heart, to sign 'love'.
Point at the other person to sign 'you'.
tip: Sign the three parts as one smooth, flowing sequence with a warm expression.

steps: Hold your dominant index finger up and wiggle it side to side with a questioning look, to sign 'what'.
Point your index finger at the person you are asking, to sign 'your'.
Touch your forehead with your index and middle fingers held together, then twist your wrist so the fingertips point forward, to sign 'name'.
tip: In BSL the topic comes first, so fluent signers often order the signs 'name' then 'what'.
